name: financial_accounting_set2_p1
label: Financial Accounting: set 2 (trial balance, errors, suspense, bank reconciliation, final accounts)

papers.title: The Trial Balance: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on the trial balance, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: The main purpose of a trial balance is to
questions.explanation:
Equal debit and credit totals show that the double entry is arithmetically correct.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- find the net profit of the business: Net profit is found in the income statement.
- show the financial position on a date: That is the statement of financial position.
- prove that the books contain no errors: Some errors are not revealed by the trial balance.

options.label: A
options.content: check the arithmetical accuracy of the double entry

options.label: B
options.content: find the net profit of the business

options.label: C
options.content: show the financial position on a date

options.label: D
options.content: prove that the books contain no errors

questions.stem: Which balance appears on the credit side of a trial balance?
questions.explanation:
Returns outwards (purchases returns) reduce purchases and are a credit balance.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- returns inwards: Returns inwards reduce sales: a debit balance.
- discount allowed: Discount allowed is an expense: a debit balance.
- drawings: Drawings are a debit balance.

questions.stem: Total debit balances are NLe 374,000 and credit balances other than capital are NLe 208,000. The capital is
questions.explanation:
Capital = 374,000 − 208,000 = 166,000.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- NLe 582,000: The two totals have been added.
- NLe 208,000: That is the credits other than capital.
- NLe 374,000: That is the debit total.

questions.stem: A rent received balance of NLe 3,000 is wrongly listed on the debit side. The trial balance totals will differ by
questions.explanation:
Debit total +3,000 and credit total −3,000, so the difference is 2 × 3,000 = 6,000.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- NLe 3,000: The debit is 3,000 too high and the credit 3,000 too low.
- NLe 1,500: The difference is twice the amount, not half.
- NLe 0: A misplaced balance always causes a difference.

questions.stem: The inventory figure in a trial balance is the
questions.explanation:
Closing inventory is found by stocktaking after the trial balance and is not yet in the ledger.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- closing inventory: Closing inventory is usually given below the trial balance.
- average inventory: The trial balance shows ledger balances, not averages.
- inventory sold during the year: That is the cost of sales.

papers.title: Errors in Accounting: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on errors in accounting, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: A purchase of a computer was debited to the purchases account. This is an error of
questions.explanation:
A non-current asset has been treated as an expense: the wrong class of account.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- commission: Commission is posting to the wrong account of the same class.
- omission: Omission is leaving a transaction out completely.
- original entry: Original entry is a wrong amount in the source book.

questions.stem: Cash received from Bah was credited to Bai's account. This is an error of
questions.explanation:
The correct amount was posted to the wrong personal account of the same class.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- principle: Principle is posting to the wrong class of account.
- complete reversal: Complete reversal swaps debit and credit.
- compensating: Compensating errors cancel each other out.

questions.stem: Which error will cause the trial balance totals to disagree?
questions.explanation:
Only one side of the entry was made, so the debits are short.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- a sale omitted from the books entirely: Omission leaves both sides out.
- a sale of 2,450 recorded as 2,540 in the day book: Original entry errors affect both sides equally.
- a payment posted to the wrong supplier's account: Commission errors keep debits equal to credits.

options.label: A
options.content: a sale omitted from the books entirely

options.label: B
options.content: a sale of 2,450 recorded as 2,540 in the day book

options.label: C
options.content: a payment posted to the wrong supplier's account

options.label: D
options.content: wages posted to the cash book but not to the wages account

questions.stem: Cash of NLe 1,500 paid to Sesay was debited to cash and credited to Sesay. The correcting entry is
questions.explanation:
The wrong entries must be cancelled and the right ones made: twice the amount.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- debit Sesay NLe 1,500, credit cash NLe 1,500: A complete reversal needs twice the amount.
- debit cash NLe 3,000, credit Sesay NLe 3,000: That doubles the error.
- debit suspense NLe 1,500, credit cash NLe 1,500: A complete reversal does not affect the suspense account.

options.label: A
options.content: debit Sesay NLe 3,000, credit cash NLe 3,000

options.label: B
options.content: debit Sesay NLe 1,500, credit cash NLe 1,500

options.label: C
options.content: debit cash NLe 3,000, credit Sesay NLe 3,000

options.label: D
options.content: debit suspense NLe 1,500, credit cash NLe 1,500

questions.stem: A credit purchase of NLe 5,600 from Bangura was recorded as NLe 6,500. The correcting entry is
questions.explanation:
Both purchases and Bangura were 900 too high (6,500 − 5,600), so both are reduced.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- debit purchases NLe 900, credit Bangura NLe 900: Both accounts are overstated and must be reduced.
- debit Bangura NLe 6,500, credit purchases NLe 6,500: Only the difference needs correcting.
- debit suspense NLe 900, credit purchases NLe 900: An original entry error does not go through suspense.

options.label: A
options.content: debit purchases NLe 900, credit Bangura NLe 900

options.label: B
options.content: debit Bangura NLe 900, credit purchases NLe 900

options.label: C
options.content: debit Bangura NLe 6,500, credit purchases NLe 6,500

options.label: D
options.content: debit suspense NLe 900, credit purchases NLe 900

papers.title: The Suspense Account: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on the suspense account, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: A trial balance shows debits of NLe 89,600 and credits of NLe 90,300. The suspense account will show
questions.explanation:
Difference = 90,300 − 89,600 = 700, added to the short (debit) side.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- a credit balance of NLe 700: The debit side is short, so suspense is debited.
- a debit balance of NLe 179,900: The totals have been added.
- no balance: A difference must be placed in suspense.

questions.stem: The sales account was undercast by NLe 200. The correcting entry is
questions.explanation:
Sales (a credit balance) needs 200 more; the other side goes to suspense.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- debit sales, credit suspense: Sales must be increased with a credit.
- debit sales, credit cash: No cash is involved.
- debit cash, credit sales: The cash book is already correct.

questions.stem: Which error would NOT be corrected through the suspense account?
questions.explanation:
Omission affects both debits and credits equally, so it never caused a difference.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- a casting error in the sales account: This affects one account and the trial balance.
- wages entered in the cash book but not posted: This is a one-sided entry.
- a balance extracted wrongly into the trial balance: This makes the trial balance disagree.

options.label: B
options.content: a casting error in the sales account

options.label: C
options.content: wages entered in the cash book but not posted

options.label: D
options.content: a balance extracted wrongly into the trial balance

questions.stem: Draft net profit is NLe 25,000. Sales were undercast by NLe 200 and wages of NLe 900 were not charged. Corrected net profit is
questions.explanation:
25,000 + 200 − 900 = 24,300.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- NLe 26,100: The wages should be deducted, not added.
- NLe 25,700: The sales should be added, not deducted, and the wages deducted.
- NLe 23,900: The sales undercast should be added, not deducted.

questions.stem: An uncleared debit balance on the suspense account at the year end appears in the
questions.explanation:
A temporary debit balance is shown with the current assets until the errors are found.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- income statement as an expense: It is not an expense.
- statement of financial position as a current liability: A credit balance would be a current liability.
- trading account: The trading account deals with sales and cost of sales.

options.label: B
options.content: statement of financial position as a current liability

options.label: C
options.content: statement of financial position as a current asset

papers.title: Bank Reconciliation: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on bank reconciliation, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: Cheques paid out and entered in the cash book but not yet presented to the bank are called
questions.explanation:
Unpresented cheques are timing differences shown in the reconciliation statement.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- uncredited lodgements: Uncredited lodgements are money paid in but not yet credited.
- dishonoured cheques: Dishonoured cheques are cheques the paying bank refused.
- standing orders: Standing orders are regular payments made by the bank.

questions.stem: Which item should be entered in the cash book when preparing an adjusted cash book?
questions.explanation:
Items the business learns about only from the bank statement are entered in the cash book first.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- unpresented cheques: These are already in the cash book.
- uncredited lodgements: These are already in the cash book.
- the bank statement balance: The bank statement balance is the target of the reconciliation.

options.label: A
options.content: bank charges shown only on the bank statement

questions.stem: The cash book shows NLe 18,400. Bank charges are NLe 350, a standing order NLe 1,200, a direct credit NLe 2,400 and a dishonoured cheque NLe 1,000. The adjusted balance is
questions.explanation:
18,400 + 2,400 − 350 − 1,200 − 1,000 = 18,250.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- NLe 23,350: Charges, standing order and dishonoured cheque must be deducted.
- NLe 20,800: Only the direct credit has been adjusted.
- NLe 13,450: The direct credit must be added, not deducted.

questions.stem: Starting from the adjusted cash book balance of NLe 18,250, add unpresented cheques of NLe 4,950 and deduct an uncredited lodgement of NLe 2,600. The bank statement balance is
questions.explanation:
18,250 + 4,950 − 2,600 = 20,600.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- NLe 15,900: Unpresented cheques must be added, not deducted.
- NLe 25,800: The uncredited lodgement must be deducted.
- NLe 10,700: The signs have been reversed.

questions.stem: The bank balance shown in the statement of financial position is the
questions.explanation:
The adjusted cash book includes every item the business has paid or received.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- bank statement balance: The bank statement has not caught up with unpresented items.
- original cash book balance: It omits items such as bank charges.
- average of the two balances: No averaging is used.

papers.title: Final Accounts of Sole Proprietorship: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on final accounts of sole proprietorship, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: Opening inventory NLe 18,000; net purchases NLe 93,000; carriage inwards NLe 1,500; closing inventory NLe 20,000. Cost of sales is
questions.explanation:
18,000 + 93,000 + 1,500 − 20,000 = 92,500.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- NLe 112,500: Closing inventory has not been deducted.
- NLe 89,500: Carriage inwards must be added, not deducted.
- NLe 132,500: Closing inventory has been added instead of deducted.

questions.stem: Carriage outwards is shown in the
questions.explanation:
Carriage outwards is the cost of delivering goods to customers: a selling expense.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- trading section as part of cost of sales: That is where carriage inwards goes.
- statement of financial position as a liability: It is an expense, not a liability.
- trading section as a deduction from sales: Returns inwards are deducted from sales.

options.label: A
options.content: trading section as part of cost of sales

options.label: B
options.content: profit and loss section as an expense

options.label: C
options.content: statement of financial position as a liability

options.label: D
options.content: trading section as a deduction from sales

questions.stem: Net sales are NLe 158,000 and gross profit is NLe 65,500. Expenses are NLe 41,500 and other income NLe 3,500. Net profit is
questions.explanation:
65,500 + 3,500 − 41,500 = 27,500.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- NLe 24,000: Other income must be added.
- NLe 65,500: That is the gross profit.
- NLe 116,500: Net sales minus expenses is not net profit.

questions.stem: Current assets are NLe 45,000 and current liabilities NLe 11,500. Working capital is
questions.explanation:
Working capital = 45,000 − 11,500 = 33,500.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- NLe 56,500: Current liabilities must be deducted.
- NLe 11,500: That is the current liabilities.
- NLe 3,500: That is not the difference between the two figures.

questions.stem: Drawings by the owner are shown in the
questions.explanation:
Closing capital = opening capital + net profit − drawings.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- income statement as an expense: Drawings are not a business expense.
- trading account as a deduction from purchases: Only goods taken affect purchases, through drawings.
- statement of financial position as a current liability: Drawings reduce capital; they are not a liability.

options.label: A
options.content: statement of financial position as a deduction from capital

options.label: C
options.content: trading account as a deduction from purchases

options.label: D
options.content: statement of financial position as a current liability

papers.title: Adjustments to Final Accounts: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on adjustments to final accounts, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: Rent paid during the year was NLe 11,000 and NLe 1,000 is owing at the year end. The rent charged in the income statement is
questions.explanation:
Expense = paid + accrued = 11,000 + 1,000 = 12,000.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- NLe 11,000: The amount owing must be added.
- NLe 10,000: An accrual is added, not deducted.
- NLe 1,000: That is only the accrual.

questions.stem: A prepaid expense at the year end is shown in the statement of financial position as
questions.explanation:
The business has paid for a benefit it has not yet received.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- a current liability: An accrued expense is a current liability.
- a non-current asset: Prepayments are short-term.
- part of capital: Prepayments are not capital.

questions.stem: A machine cost NLe 100,000. Depreciation is 30% a year on the reducing balance. The charge for year 2 is
questions.explanation:
Year 1: 30,000, carrying amount 70,000. Year 2: 30% × 70,000 = 21,000.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- NLe 30,000: That is the year 1 charge.
- NLe 20,000: That is 20% straight line.
- NLe 49,000: That is the carrying amount after year 2.

questions.stem: Receivables are NLe 39,000 after bad debts. A 5% provision is required and the existing provision is NLe 1,500. The charge to the income statement is
questions.explanation:
New provision 5% × 39,000 = 1,950; increase = 1,950 − 1,500 = 450.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- NLe 1,950: Only the increase is charged.
- NLe 1,500: That is the old provision.
- NLe 3,450: The old provision is deducted, not added.

questions.stem: Under the straight-line method, depreciation each year is calculated as
questions.explanation:
Straight line spreads the depreciable amount equally over the asset's useful life.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- a fixed percentage of the carrying amount: That is the reducing-balance method.
- cost × useful life: That would exceed the cost.
- residual value ÷ useful life: The depreciable amount is cost less residual value.

options.label: A
options.content: a fixed percentage of the carrying amount

papers.title: Stock Valuation: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on stock valuation, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: Under FIFO, closing inventory is valued at
questions.explanation:
The oldest goods are assumed sold first, so those left are the most recent purchases.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the earliest purchase prices: That is LIFO.
- the average purchase price: That is AVCO.
- the selling price: Inventory is valued at cost, not selling price.

questions.stem: When prices are rising, which method gives the highest gross profit?
questions.explanation:
FIFO charges older, cheaper costs to cost of sales, so profit is highest.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- LIFO: LIFO gives the lowest profit when prices rise.
- AVCO: AVCO gives a profit between FIFO and LIFO.
- all give the same profit: The methods give different closing inventories.

questions.stem: A business holds 50 units at NLe 50 and buys 50 more at NLe 62. Using AVCO, the average cost per unit is
questions.explanation:
Total cost = 2,500 + 3,100 = 5,600 for 100 units, so 56 per unit.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- NLe 62: That is the latest price.
- NLe 50: That is the earliest price.
- NLe 112: That adds the two prices.

questions.stem: An item cost NLe 4,000. It can be sold for NLe 3,200 after repairs costing NLe 500. It should be valued at
questions.explanation:
NRV = 3,200 − 500 = 2,700, which is below cost, so value = 2,700.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- NLe 4,000: Net realisable value is lower than cost.
- NLe 3,200: Repair costs must be deducted.
- NLe 3,700: Selling costs are deducted from the selling price, not from cost.

questions.stem: If closing inventory is overstated, gross profit for the year is
questions.explanation:
Higher closing inventory → lower cost of sales → higher gross profit.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- understated: A higher closing inventory lowers cost of sales.
- unaffected: Closing inventory affects cost of sales.
- doubled: It changes by the amount of the error, not double.

papers.title: Manufacturing Accounts: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on manufacturing accounts, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: Prime cost is
questions.explanation:
Prime cost is the total of the direct costs of production.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- direct materials + factory overheads: Factory overheads are added after prime cost.
- production cost + office expenses: Office expenses go to the profit and loss section.
- sales − cost of sales: That is gross profit.

options.label: D
options.content: direct materials consumed + direct labour + direct expenses

questions.stem: Which of the following is a factory overhead?
questions.explanation:
Factory overheads are indirect manufacturing costs.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- wages of machine operators: These are direct labour.
- raw materials used: These are direct materials.
- office salaries: These are administration expenses.

questions.stem: Opening raw materials NLe 12,000; purchases NLe 80,000; carriage inwards NLe 2,000; closing raw materials NLe 15,000. Raw materials consumed is
questions.explanation:
12,000 + 80,000 + 2,000 − 15,000 = 79,000.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- NLe 94,000: Closing raw materials must be deducted.
- NLe 75,000: Carriage inwards must be added.
- NLe 109,000: Closing raw materials must be deducted, not added.

questions.stem: Prime cost NLe 127,000; factory overheads NLe 35,000; opening WIP NLe 7,000; closing WIP NLe 9,000. Production cost is
questions.explanation:
127,000 + 35,000 + 7,000 − 9,000 = 160,000.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- NLe 162,000: The work in progress adjustment is missing.
- NLe 178,000: Closing WIP must be deducted, not added.
- NLe 146,000: Opening WIP must be added, not deducted.

questions.stem: The production cost of goods completed is transferred to the
questions.explanation:
A manufacturer makes rather than buys its goods, so production cost replaces purchases.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- statement of financial position: It is a cost, not an asset.
- profit and loss section as an expense: It belongs in cost of sales.
- capital account: Capital is not involved.

options.label: B
options.content: profit and loss section as an expense

options.label: D
options.content: trading account, in place of purchases
